readAloud.text: As freshwater supplies come under growing pressure, many coastal nations are turning to desalination, the removal of salt from seawater. Modern plants force water through fine membranes at high pressure, producing millions of litres of drinking water every day. The technology is reliable but costly, and disposing of the leftover brine without damaging marine life remains a significant environmental challenge.

High-speed rail has transformed long-distance travel in countries that have invested in it. Trains travelling at three hundred kilometres per hour can compete directly with airlines on journeys of up to four hours, especially because stations are located in city centres. Supporters also point out that electrified railways produce far lower emissions per passenger than either cars or planes.

Food fraud costs the global economy billions of dollars each year, and honey is among the most commonly faked products. Unscrupulous suppliers dilute pure honey with cheap sugar syrups or mislabel its country of origin to avoid import duties. Because many syrups are chemically similar to honey, laboratories must use advanced techniques, including DNA analysis and isotope testing, to expose the deception.

Avalanche forecasters combine field observations with weather data to estimate the stability of the snowpack. They dig pits in the snow to examine individual layers, searching for weak crystals that could collapse under the weight of fresh snowfall. Their daily bulletins, which rate the danger on a five-point scale, help skiers and rescue services decide where travel is acceptably safe.

Telehealth, the delivery of medical care through video calls and remote monitoring, expanded rapidly during the pandemic and has since become a permanent feature of healthcare. It is particularly valuable for patients in rural areas, who might otherwise travel for hours to see a specialist. Nevertheless, doctors acknowledge that some conditions can only be assessed properly through a physical examination.

Street art has undergone a remarkable change in status over the past four decades. Murals that were once scrubbed away as vandalism are now protected by local councils, and works by famous street artists sell for millions at international auctions. Some critics worry, however, that commercial success and official approval have drained the movement of the rebellious energy that made it powerful.

Co-working spaces have multiplied in cities around the world, offering freelancers and remote employees an alternative to working alone at home. For a monthly fee, members receive a desk, fast internet, and access to meeting rooms, as well as opportunities to network with people from other industries. Surveys suggest many members join primarily to escape isolation and rebuild a boundary between work and home life.

retellLecture.title: How avalanche forecasting saves lives
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained that most fatal avalanches are triggered by the victims themselves or their companions rather than occurring randomly. Forecasters examine snowpack layers for weak crystals that may collapse under the weight of new snow. The speaker stressed that survival depends on education and on carrying three essentials: a transceiver, a probe and a shovel. Finally, the lecture noted that most buried survivors are dug out by companions within fifteen minutes.
retellLecture.text: Avalanches kill around one hundred and fifty people worldwide every winter, yet most fatal slides are not random acts of nature. In roughly ninety percent of cases, the victim or someone in their group triggers the avalanche. The key to survival, therefore, lies in education and preparation. Forecasters assess the snowpack layer by layer, looking for weak, sugary crystals that can collapse suddenly under the weight of new snow. Before heading into the backcountry, every skier should carry three essential items: a transceiver, which sends out a radio signal, a probe for pinpointing a buried person, and a shovel, because most survivors are dug out by companions within fifteen minutes.

retellLecture.title: The global problem of fake honey
retellLecture.sample: The lecture described honey as the third most faked food in the world, after milk and olive oil. Fraudsters feed bees sugar syrup, harvest the honey too early, or blend in cheap rice and corn syrups. Because these syrups resemble genuine honey chemically, basic laboratory tests often fail to detect them, so regulators now use nuclear magnetic resonance profiling. The speaker concluded that cheap adulterated imports are driving honest beekeepers out of business.
retellLecture.text: Honey is the third most faked food in the world, after milk and olive oil. Fraud takes several forms. Producers may feed bees sugar syrup instead of letting them forage, harvest the honey too early, or stretch supplies by blending in cheap rice or corn syrup. Because these syrups are made from plants similar to those bees visit, basic laboratory tests often fail to detect them. Regulators have turned to more sophisticated methods, such as nuclear magnetic resonance profiling, which compares a sample's chemical fingerprint against a database of genuine honeys. The economic stakes are high: cheap adulterated imports undercut honest beekeepers and have driven many producers out of business.

respondToSituation.prompt: Your flight to another city has just been cancelled, and you have a job interview there at ten o'clock tomorrow morning. You are now at the airline's service desk. Speak to the airline agent. What would you say?
respondToSituation.audio: Your flight to another city has just been cancelled, and you have a job interview there at ten o'clock tomorrow morning. You are now at the airline's service desk. Speak to the airline agent. What would you say?
respondToSituation.sample: Good morning, I really need your help. I was booked on the eight o'clock flight to Manchester, and it's just been cancelled. The problem is I have a job interview tomorrow at ten a.m., and this job means a lot to me. Could you please check if there's any seat left on another flight this evening — with any airline, I'm not fussy? If flying is impossible, would the airline cover a train ticket, or a hotel near the airport so I can take the first flight in the morning? I'd also like to know how to claim compensation, since the cancellation was the airline's fault. I understand this isn't your doing personally, and I really do appreciate whatever you can arrange. Thank you so much.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should companies replace human customer-service staff with chatbots?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The group debated replacing customer-service staff with chatbots. Speaker A favoured chatbots because they answer instantly, work around the clock, and are faster than waiting on hold for simple queries. Speaker B objected that bots fail on unusual problems, frustrate customers, and threaten call-centre jobs. Speaker C proposed a hybrid model in which bots handle routine queries and pass complex cases to humans along with the conversation history. In the end, all three converged on keeping an easy route to a human and retraining affected staff.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honestly, I think chatbots are brilliant for most customer queries. They answer instantly, they're available at midnight, and they never lose their temper. For simple things like tracking an order or resetting a password, a bot is far faster than waiting forty minutes on hold.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I'd push back on that. The moment your problem is slightly unusual, the bot just loops the same useless answers, and it's infuriating. And let's not forget the human cost — call centres employ millions of people. Companies are basically swapping decent service for lower wage bills.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Isn't the answer a hybrid system? Let the bots handle the routine seventy percent of queries and hand anything complex to trained humans. My bank does that, and it works pretty well — the bot even passes the conversation history so you don't have to repeat yourself.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That handover point is crucial, though. If the transition to a human is smooth, fine — but some companies make it deliberately hard to reach a real person.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. I'd support chatbots if companies were required to offer a speak-to-a-human button at all times, and if the savings went into retraining staff rather than pure profit.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: So we basically agree: bots for the simple tasks, guaranteed human backup, and some protection for the workers whose jobs change.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: The government must choose between funding a high-speed rail line and expanding the city's airport. Which should get the money?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The speakers weighed a high-speed rail line against airport expansion. Speaker A championed rail for its lower emissions, central stations, and faster door-to-door times on short journeys. Speaker B defended the airport, stressing global connections, job creation, and cleaner aviation fuels. Speaker C supported rail because airport growth is concentrated in the short-haul market that trains can replace, while noting long-haul capacity is already sufficient. They ultimately agreed to prioritise rail while still funding compulsory airport safety upgrades.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'd put the money into high-speed rail without hesitation. Trains emit a fraction of the carbon of planes, stations are in the city centre, and on journeys under four hours, rail is actually quicker door-to-door. Half the flights from our airport are short-haul routes a train could easily replace.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: But the airport connects us to the rest of the world — rail can't fly you to Singapore or New York. Expansion would create thousands of jobs and attract international companies. And airlines are investing in cleaner fuels, so the environmental argument won't always be this one-sided.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: You both assume it's either-or, but the budget is fixed. I lean towards rail, mainly because the airport's own figures show most of its growth is in the short-haul market — precisely the part rail can absorb. Long-haul capacity matters, but we already have enough of it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Plus, rail construction creates jobs too, and the benefits flow to the regional cities along the line, not just the capital.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Fair point. I could accept rail first — as long as the airport's safety upgrades, which are compulsory anyway, still go ahead.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Agreed. Fund the rail line, keep the essential airport maintenance, and revisit expansion in five years.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Elite sport has embraced sleep science with remarkable enthusiasm in recent years. Studies show that extending sleep to nine or ten hours a night improves sprint times, shooting accuracy, and reaction speed in athletes across a range of sports, while even modest sleep deprivation measurably slows decision-making and increases injury risk. Sleep is when the body releases growth hormone and repairs the microscopic muscle damage caused by training, so skimping on rest undermines the very adaptations that training is designed to produce. Many professional teams now employ sleep coaches, provide players with personalised sleep schedules, and have redesigned travel arrangements so that athletes cross fewer time zones before important matches. Some researchers argue that sleep offers the largest legal performance advantage still available in modern sport.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Because sleep improves athletic performance, speeds recovery and reduces injuries while deprivation undermines training, professional teams increasingly employ sleep coaches, personalised schedules and adjusted travel plans, leading some researchers to describe sleep as the greatest legal performance advantage remaining in sport.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Telehealth — consultations conducted by telephone or video — moved from the margins of medicine to the mainstream almost overnight during the COVID-19 pandemic, and much of that shift appears permanent. The benefits are clearest for routine care: repeat prescriptions, mental-health check-ins, and follow-up appointments can be handled without travel, saving time for patients and clinics alike. Rural communities, where specialists may be hundreds of kilometres away, gain access that geography once denied them. Yet the model has boundaries. A camera cannot feel an abdomen, listen closely to a chest, or take blood, and video quality depends on internet connections that remain unreliable in many regions. Most clinicians therefore envisage a blended future, in which telehealth handles appropriate cases while physical examinations remain reserved for those who genuinely need them.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Although telehealth expanded rapidly during the pandemic and offers clear benefits for routine care and rural access, its inability to perform physical examinations and its dependence on reliable internet mean most clinicians favour a blended model combining remote consultations with in-person care.

essay.prompt: Some people regard graffiti and street art as a legitimate form of artistic expression, while others see it as vandalism that should be punished. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write 200–300 words.
essay.sample: Possible structure: (1) Introduction — paraphrase the debate, state your position, e.g. street art can be legitimate art when done with permission. (2) Case for street art: transforms dull public spaces, gives a voice to marginalised groups, is recognised by galleries and auction houses, and cities like Berlin and Melbourne attract tourists with their murals. (3) Case against: tagging and unwanted graffiti damage private property, cost councils millions to clean, and make areas feel neglected. (4) Conclusion — your view, e.g. legal walls and commissioned murals preserve the creativity while removing the harm. Useful phrases: 'It is often claimed that…', 'Supporters of street art point out that…', 'Critics, however, argue…', 'A balanced view would be…', 'In conclusion, I believe…'

In Japan and Mexico, such systems already give residents precious seconds to take cover.

summarizeSpokenText.title: Sleep: the athlete's legal performance enhancer
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The speaker explained that sports science has reversed the old habit of waking athletes at dawn. In one study, basketball players who slept ten hours improved their sprint times and shooting accuracy. Sleep is active recovery, releasing growth hormone and consolidating skills, while even partial sleep deprivation slows reactions and doubles injury rates. Consequently, professional teams now hire sleep consultants, schedule later training after late matches, and plan travel to minimise jet lag.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Coaches once bragged about waking players at dawn, but sports science has reversed that thinking. When basketball players in one study extended their sleep to ten hours a night, their sprint times and shooting accuracy improved significantly, and they reported feeling better. Sleep is not passive recovery; it is when the body releases growth hormone and consolidates the skills practised during training. Even partial sleep deprivation slows reaction times and doubles injury rates in adolescents. For this reason, professional teams now hire sleep consultants, schedule later training sessions after late matches, and design travel plans that minimise jet lag. Sleep, in short, has become the last legal performance enhancer.

summarizeSpokenText.title: Why food allergies are on the rise
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture noted that food allergies are far more common than in the past, with hospital admissions for severe reactions tripling in some countries and peanut allergy affecting about two percent of children. The leading explanation, the hygiene hypothesis, blames overly clean homes that leave young immune systems undertrained, while other researchers point to changes in infant feeding, since early introduction of peanuts lowered allergy rates. Whatever the cause, the trend has transformed school lunches and food labelling laws.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Food allergies are far more common than they used to be, and the statistics agree. Hospital admissions for severe allergic reactions have tripled in some countries over the past twenty years, and peanut allergy alone now affects around two percent of children. Why this is happening is less clear. The leading explanation, the hygiene hypothesis, argues that modern homes are so clean that young immune systems, deprived of contact with dirt and microbes, mistake harmless foods for threats. Other researchers point to changes in infant feeding, noting that countries which introduced peanuts early saw allergy rates fall. Whatever the cause, the trend has transformed school lunches and food labelling laws.
